newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda detains more than 2,300 Hutu returnees.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda detains more than 2,300 Hutu returnees.

text.p: Rwandan authorities have detained more than 2,300 returning Hutu refugees suspected of involvement in the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis, the U.N. human rights agency said on Tuesday.
Rwanda's justice ministry said the first trials of some 90,000 suspects held in jails accused of genocide open on Friday in southeast Rwanda and next Monday in the capital Kigali.

Those found guilty of being ringleaders or killers of large numbers, or having used especially brutal methods in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates, could face the death penalty.

The Kigali office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights said Rwandan authorities had detained more than 1,680 Hutu refugees who were herded out of Tanzania this month and 700 returnees who fled fighting in Zaire last month.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) expressed concern at the detentions.

"Detained, rather than arrested, is the best word because these include a lot of people in protective custody to guard against vigilante violence," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg. "But it appears to be increasing day by day."
An estimated 600,000 Hutus returned to their homeland from camps in Zaire last month after being caught up in fighting between exiled Rwandan militia and Zairean Tutsi rebels.
About 388,000 have returned from Tanzania this month ahead of a December 31 deadline imposed by the Tanzanian authorities on all 542,000 refugees to leave.
Fear of arrest in Rwanda and intimidation by Hutu hardliners had prevented many from returning earlier.

Many Hutu militiamen who fled Rwanda as Tutsi rebels swept them from power after the genocide in 1994 have moved deeper into Zaire and Tanzania rather than return to face justice or reprisal killings in Rwanda.
Rwandan justice ministry director Gerald Gahima said the first accused of genocide would face a tribunal on Friday at Kibungo, 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Kigali.
"I believe there are two accused. It will be a slow start and things will pick up as we go along. We hope that by next month all 12 tribunals will be working across Rwanda," he told Reuters.

Authorities did not plan to put all those held in Rwandan prisons on trial. "Our suspicion is that a majority may respond to our confession programme and receive some measure of leniency," Gahima added.
Evidence gathered in the past two years would be presented to panels of three judges in the trials which are expected to last several days each. Then there is one chance of appeal.

"The very worst offenders are out of the country, and some of those before the tribunals may not be high-ranking. But the bottom line is they must be seen to be punished, that you cannot get away with these kind of crimes for any reason," Gahima said.

A Hutu refugee lobby group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda, has dismissed the trials as "a parody of justice" and said the returnees being detained were being falsely accused by people who wanted their property.
